trails.bestSeason: Apr-Oct; South Rim Road beyond the visitor center closes in winter
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, South Rim Road closes to vehicles beyond the visitor center around mid-November and typically stays closed into late April, so reaching the Warner Point trailhead in winter requires walking, skiing, or snowshoeing the closed road.
trails.didYouKnow: Warner Point overlooks the deepest and narrowest section of the canyon, where the walls plunge nearly 2,700 feet to the Gunnison River.

trails.trailTip: This loop dips just below the canyon rim into a Gambel oak forest — footing includes some rocky, uneven sections, so wear sturdy shoes.
trails.didYouKnow: Oak Flat is one of the only maintained trails that goes below the canyon rim without requiring a wilderness permit, making it a good introduction to the canyon's terrain.

trails.trailTip: A short walk to the canyon's narrowest point, where the rims are less than 1,300 feet apart — hold onto kids near the unfenced edge.
trails.didYouKnow: Chasm View looks across the canyon's narrowest gap, and it's possible to see (and sometimes hear) hikers on the opposite North Rim trail.

trails.trailTip: A quieter, rolling trail through pinyon-juniper woodland on the less-visited North Rim — carry water, since there's no shade relief for long stretches.
trails.didYouKnow: The North Rim sees a fraction of the visitors the South Rim does, making the Uplands Trail one of the best options in the park for solitude.

trails.bestSeason: May-Oct; permits released in two Recreation.gov windows
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this South Rim inner-canyon route requires a Wilderness Use Permit reserved on Recreation.gov (the April 1 window opens May-July dates, the July 1 window opens August-October dates; off-season permits are available in person at the South Rim Visitor Center), and hikers should expect hazardous burned-area conditions — steep unstable slopes, loose rock, and burned vegetation — left by the 2025 South Rim Fire.
trails.didYouKnow: Considered the easiest of the inner canyon routes, the Gunnison Route is still a steep, unmaintained 1,800-foot descent that typically requires hands as well as feet on the way back up.

trails.trailTip: This North Rim trail to Exclamation Point and Green Mountain has no shade for much of its length — start early in warmer months and carry more water than usual.
trails.didYouKnow: Exclamation Point, just over a mile in, is considered one of the best canyon overlooks in the park and a worthwhile shorter turnaround if you don't have time for the full trail.

trails.trailTip: An easy walk near the South Rim Visitor Center connecting several overlooks — a good option for a quick look at the canyon without committing to a longer hike.
trails.didYouKnow: This trail links several of the South Rim's most accessible overlooks, making it possible to see multiple canyon views without driving between pullouts.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this North Rim inner-canyon route requires a free Wilderness Use Permit, available first-come, first-served the evening before or morning of your hike at the North Rim Ranger Station, with roughly 15 permits issued per day and a mandatory ranger safety briefing.
trails.didYouKnow: SOB Draw is one of only a couple of access points into the canyon from the North Rim, and its name is a fair warning about the steep, loose terrain involved.

animals.whereToLook: Sheer cliff walls throughout the canyon, especially near Painted Wall and Serpent Point
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, the park closes specific climbing routes near known peregrine eyries — including areas around Painted Wall and Serpent Point on the North Rim, and routes upstream of Echo Canyon on the South Rim — from roughly March 15 through July 15 each year; view nesting falcons from established overlooks with binoculars rather than climbing near a cliff face during this window.
animals.didYouKnow: Painted Wall, Colorado's tallest cliff at over 2,250 feet, is prime peregrine nesting habitat and one of the best places in the park to watch them hunt.

animals.whereToLook: Rim thermals throughout the park, especially near overlooks on both rims
animals.viewingTip: Scan the rim thermals with binoculars from established overlooks, and keep well back from any cliff-face nest, since golden eagles will abandon a nest site if repeatedly disturbed.
animals.didYouKnow: Golden eagles can spot prey from over a mile away and are capable of taking down animals as large as young deer.

animals.viewingTip: Mule deer are commonly seen from park roads and overlooks — watch from a pullout with binoculars, and give extra space to bucks during the fall rut when they're more unpredictable.
animals.didYouKnow: Mule deer can jump all four feet off the ground simultaneously in a bounding gait called "stotting," useful for navigating the park's rocky terrain.

animals.whereToLook: Gambel oak brush along both rims, especially near campgrounds
animals.viewingTip: View any bear from a safe distance with binoculars and store all food and scented items in the bear-proof lockers provided at campgrounds — a bear that gets human food often has to be relocated or destroyed.
animals.didYouKnow: Black bears fatten up on Gambel oak acorns each late summer and fall, sometimes traveling long distances between the park's rims to find a good acorn crop.

animals.whereToLook: Steep canyon walls, most reliably viewed from East Portal Road
animals.viewingTip: Scan the canyon walls from East Portal Road pullouts with binoculars, and give rutting rams extra distance in fall — a startled sheep on that terrain risks a serious fall, not just a spoiled photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Black Canyon's bighorn sheep were reintroduced in the 1980s and now use the canyon's sheer walls as natural protection from predators.

animals.whereToLook: Open meadows along both the North and South Rim
animals.viewingTip: Watch rim meadows at dawn or dusk with binoculars, and stay well back from bulls during the fall rut, when they're aggressive and unpredictable and should never be approached for a photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Bull elk bugles during the September-October rut can carry for over a mile across the canyon's open rim country.

animals.whereToLook: Rim thermals and open pinyon-juniper woodland along park roads
animals.viewingTip: Look up along the rim roads for hawks riding thermals or perched on snags, watching with binoculars rather than approaching a perched bird too closely.
animals.didYouKnow: Red-tailed hawks' piercing scream is so recognizable it's used as the generic "eagle cry" sound effect in countless movies, regardless of what bird is actually on screen.

animals.whereToLook: Sagebrush habitat in the Gunnison Basin near the park, not typically within the canyon itself
animals.viewingTip: This species isn't reliably seen inside the canyon itself — nearby Gunnison Basin viewing sites run guided, distance-controlled lek tours each spring, and observers should always stay in a vehicle or designated viewing area rather than approaching a display ground, since disturbance can cause grouse to abandon a lek entirely.
animals.didYouKnow: First described as a distinct species in 2000, the Gunnison sage-grouse is one of the most endangered birds in North America, with the vast majority of its population found only in the Gunnison Basin.
